paragraphs: When several objectives compete, optimization often needs to produce a collection of useful compromises. A Pareto set contains candidates for which improving one objective requires sacrificing another. A-GPS learns to generate such candidates in discrete search spaces where objective values must be obtained through black-box evaluations. It also lets users express preferences after training, making the learned collection useful for different trade-offs.

The method uses a class probability estimator to predict non-dominance relations between candidates. Those predictions guide generation toward promising regions. The authors show that this estimator also implicitly estimates the probability of hypervolume improvement, allowing the approach to avoid explicitly computing hypervolume. Preference direction vectors describe which combinations of objectives a user favors.

During optimization, the model is updated using both Pareto membership and alignment with these directions. The resulting generator can sample different parts of the Pareto front without retraining for each preference. Experiments on synthetic benchmarks and protein design tasks report strong sample efficiency and effective preference incorporation, supporting the value of sharing one learned generator across multiple desired compromises.
neurips-2025-amortized-active-generation.tldr: A-GPS learns a reusable generator of promising objective trade-offs that can accommodate different user preferences without retraining.

paragraphs: A hallucination detector can examine a language model’s internal activations for evidence that generated text is unreliable. Traditional probing classifiers inspect individual combinations of a layer and a token. This gives them a narrow view of the computation, and their dependence on a particular language model makes reuse across models difficult.

ACT-ViT instead treats the full activation tensor as an image-like object. Layers and token positions provide two ordered axes, so the detector can consider patterns across both the processing depth and the generated sequence. Its architecture draws on Vision Transformers and supports training on activations collected from multiple language models together.

Across the evaluated models and datasets, ACT-ViT consistently outperforms traditional probes while remaining efficient to deploy. Joint training with multiple language models substantially improves its performance. The authors also report strong zero-shot results on unseen datasets and effective adaptation to new language models through fine-tuning. These are distinct findings: dataset transfer works without additional training in the reported tests, whereas transfer to new language models uses fine-tuning.
neurips-2025-beyond-token-probes-halluci.tldr: ACT-ViT detects hallucinations by analyzing activation patterns across layers and tokens, benefiting from training on multiple language models.

paragraphs: Recovering a network from data can require understanding relationships at two scales simultaneously. Individual components may interact, while larger groups organize those components. The paper targets settings where these relationships are also nonlinear, making a flat network with restrictive linear assumptions an inadequate representation of the system.

NNBLNet uses neural networks to infer both levels together. Its hierarchical selection layers apply adaptive sparsity constraints, controlling which connections remain while keeping group-level relationships consistent with their constituent connections. A compositional neural architecture learns nonlinear associations across the levels through constrained transformations. The hierarchy therefore shapes the learned network rather than being added only after estimation.

The authors establish theoretical guarantees for consistent recovery of both the higher-level connections and the lower-level structures within them under the statistical regimes they analyze. Tests on synthetic and real-world data report higher F1 scores than competing methods. The contribution combines flexible nonlinear modeling with an interpretable two-level structure, so the estimated result describes both broad organization and the detailed connections supporting it.
neurips-2025-bilevel-network-learning-vi.tldr: NNBLNet recovers nonlinear networks at two connected levels using hierarchical sparsity, with theoretical recovery guarantees and improved empirical F1 scores.

paragraphs: Protecting an entity in relational data is complicated because that entity can appear in many relationships. Its influence on training may therefore extend across multiple examples. The paper addresses this difficulty alongside another: relational training can use several interdependent sampling stages, for which standard privacy amplification analyses do not directly apply.

The proposed framework adapts differentially private stochastic gradient descent to these conditions. A sensitivity analysis tracks how entity participation affects the training computation. An adaptive gradient clipping scheme then changes clipping thresholds according to how frequently an entity occurs, connecting the control of gradient contributions to the structure of the relational data.

The authors also extend privacy amplification analysis to a specific tractable class of coupled sampling procedures, where dependence arises only through sample sizes. Together, these results provide a tailored training method with formal entity-level privacy guarantees. Experiments fine-tuning text encoders on networks with textual attributes show strong utility–privacy trade-offs. The sampling restriction matters because the theoretical extension covers that subclass, rather than every possible dependence between sampling stages.
neurips-2025-differentially-private-rela.tldr: The paper adapts private gradient training to relational data by accounting for repeated entities and a restricted class of interdependent sampling procedures.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove learned information from a trained model. Its practical usefulness depends on whether the procedure works reliably across operating conditions. This paper begins by empirically showing that popular unlearning methods can be unstable and perform poorly in different scenarios, with substantial sensitivity to hyperparameter choices.

DualOptim addresses the optimization process underlying unlearning. It combines adaptive learning rates with decoupled momentum factors. Learning rates govern update size, while momentum carries information from preceding updates. By adapting the former and separating the latter, the framework changes how unlearning updates are controlled. The proposed contribution is designed to strengthen existing unlearning algorithms.

The authors provide both empirical and theoretical evidence that DualOptim contributes to effective, stable unlearning. Their experiments span image classification, image generation, and large language models, and report substantial improvements in efficacy and stability. This breadth supports its usefulness across different kinds of models and tasks. The stated result is improved robustness of the unlearning process, rather than a claim that hyperparameter choices cease to matter.
neurips-2025-dualoptim-enhancing-efficac.tldr: DualOptim uses adaptive learning rates and decoupled momentum to improve the effectiveness and stability of existing machine unlearning algorithms.

paragraphs: Flexible docking predicts how a small molecule and a protein arrange themselves when binding, allowing both structures to change. Diffusion-based approaches generate candidate arrangements through repeated sampling and then rely on separate scoring functions to select poses. Those stages create computational overhead in a workflow intended to support drug discovery.

FIGRDock uses initial docking poses from conventional tools as a starting point. From them, it distills distance patterns that encode interactions between the molecule and protein. These patterns become explicit structural conditions for a regression model, which directly predicts the final complex. The final prediction therefore uses a single inference step without iterative sampling or an external scoring stage.

On standard benchmarks, the authors report consistently higher accuracy than the diffusion-based docking methods they compare against, alongside inference speedups of up to 100 times. That maximum speedup is a reported experimental result, not a uniform rate for every case. The findings suggest a potentially more scalable docking pipeline by combining interaction information from initial poses with direct prediction of the flexible complex.
neurips-2025-figrdock-fast-interaction-g.tldr: FIGRDock directly predicts flexible protein–ligand complexes from interaction-aware distance patterns, reporting better accuracy and up to 100-fold faster inference than diffusion methods.

paragraphs: Reasoning models often learn to map a whole problem directly to its answer. Such training can produce useful heuristics while leaving the model poorly prepared for problems larger or more complicated than its training examples. This paper instead learns how to evaluate possible solutions to smaller, manageable subproblems.

Each learned energy function defines a landscape over a subproblem’s possible solutions, with minimization providing a way to search for favorable candidates. At test time, the method combines several of these functions into a global landscape for the full problem. Additional constraints can enter during inference, allowing the constructed objective to represent problems of increasing difficulty without requiring a direct learned mapping for each complete problem.

The authors introduce Parallel Energy Minimization to improve the quality of samples drawn from the combined landscape. Across a broad collection of reasoning problems, the approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods and generalizes to larger, more complex instances. These results support the idea that reusable local solution criteria can provide a basis for reasoning beyond the complexity seen during training.
neurips-2025-generalizable-reasoning-thr.tldr: The method solves harder reasoning problems by composing energy functions learned on smaller subproblems and searching the resulting landscape.

paragraphs: Graph domain adaptation addresses a mismatch between the graphs available for training and those encountered in a target setting. Many approaches change the model or its training procedure, but severe distribution shifts and limited computation remain difficult. GRADATE approaches the problem through the choice of training data itself.

The framework selects source-domain samples for a target-domain classification task using optimal transport theory to capture distribution changes. Selection does not depend on a graph neural network’s predictions or on a particular training recipe. Here, model-free describes the selection process: the chosen data can still be used to train a model for the downstream task.

This independence makes GRADATE compatible with existing approaches that adapt the model. Experiments cover several real-world graph-level datasets and multiple types of covariate shift. The authors report that it beats existing selection methods and improves off-the-shelf graph adaptation methods while using much less training data. The findings show that choosing a more suitable source subset can complement architectural or training changes and improve data efficiency under the tested shifts.
neurips-2025-graph-data-selection-for-do.tldr: GRADATE uses optimal transport to select useful source graphs without model predictions, improving adaptation while requiring less training data.

paragraphs: An ensemble can estimate uncertainty through variation among its members, but maintaining many deep networks consumes substantial computation and memory. Compressing that ensemble into smaller models can reduce this variation and lose useful uncertainty information. The paper asks how to preserve the ensemble’s distributional behavior during compression.

Gaussian distillation represents the teacher ensemble with a student distribution. It treats each teacher network as a realization of a stochastic process and estimates the ensemble’s distribution using a deep latent factor model, a particular Gaussian process. Its mean describes the central prediction, while its covariance represents variation and how that variation is related. An expectation-maximization procedure estimates these functions stably.

Across multiple benchmark datasets, the authors report better performance than existing distillation baselines. They also demonstrate that the approach works well for language-model fine-tuning and distribution shift problems. The contribution is a way to make uncertainty itself a target of compression, preserving more than a central prediction while addressing the deployment burden that motivates replacing a full ensemble.
neurips-2025-knowledge-distillation-of-u.tldr: Gaussian distillation compresses an ensemble into a learned probability distribution to better preserve its predictive uncertainty.

paragraphs: In class-incremental learning, a vision model must recognize newly introduced categories while retaining earlier ones. Even pretrained models can lose the detailed distinctions between old categories as learning progresses. KG-GMM addresses this problem by maintaining an evolving knowledge graph that records relationships useful for recognizing classes.

During learning, the model enriches class labels with relationships from the graph. Similar categories receive different relations to make their descriptions easier to distinguish. This supplies relational cues alongside category identity, giving the model additional ways to represent distinctions that might otherwise fade as it learns new classes.

At test time, Knowledge Graph Augmented Inference examines relationships in the model’s generated text to identify specific categories. The authors report that this relational information helps correct mispredictions and reduces the loss of details about old classes. Experiments achieve state-of-the-art results in both conventional and few-shot class-incremental learning. The approach therefore uses the graph throughout learning and inference, with the reported gains supporting relational structure as a useful aid to retaining category knowledge.
neurips-2025-knowledge-graph-enhanced-ge.tldr: KG-GMM uses an evolving knowledge graph to enrich class descriptions and interpret generated text, helping retain old categories as new ones are learned.

paragraphs: Sparse snapshots reveal how a system is distributed at a few times, but leave its intervening evolution unknown. Existing bridge and flow matching methods often connect adjacent snapshots in pairs. That local construction can make it difficult to capture dependencies spanning longer periods and may reduce the coherence of inferred trajectories.

3MSBM constructs stochastic dynamics subject to multiple positional constraints together. It lifts the problem into phase space, incorporating momentum, and learns smooth curves of probability distributions. The formulation generalizes stochastic bridges to condition on several points, producing a multi-marginal stochastic optimal control problem. After fixing the path induced by the conditional bridge, a variational objective trains the underlying dynamics.

The learned transport maps preserve intermediate marginals throughout training, meaning that the distributions at intermediate constraints remain part of the matching process. The authors report improved convergence and scalability, together with superior performance across real-world applications involving temporal dependencies. The contribution brings several snapshots into one trajectory-learning framework, providing a way to model relationships that adjacent-pair interpolation can struggle to capture.
neurips-2025-momentum-multi-marginal-sch.tldr: 3MSBM learns smooth stochastic dynamics constrained by multiple snapshots, improving the modeling of long-range temporal dependencies.

paragraphs: Many multimodal language models connect a separately pretrained vision encoder to a separately pretrained language model. Because these components have different training histories, studying how the combined system scales is difficult. This paper examines native, end-to-end multimodal training under a practical constraint: the amount of available data is limited.

The authors systematically study architectural choices and identify the meta-architecture that best balances performance and training cost in their investigation. They then examine how the visual encoder and language model scale together, finding a positively correlated scaling relationship. The result treats the sizes of the two components as connected design choices within the jointly trained system.

These findings lead to NaViL, a native multimodal model paired with a simple, cost-effective training recipe. Evaluation on 14 multimodal benchmarks shows competitive performance against existing models. The paper contributes both a working model and empirical guidance about allocating model capacity under data constraints. Its architectural conclusions come from the studied design space and setting, while the benchmark results establish competitiveness rather than uniform superiority.
neurips-2025-navil-rethinking-scaling-pr.tldr: NaViL studies joint vision–language scaling under limited data and turns its findings into a competitively performing native multimodal model.

paragraphs: Graph prompt learning adapts pretrained graph models to downstream tasks, but prompts can intervene at very different places: inputs, internal layers, or final representations. This makes their underlying role difficult to compare. Existing approaches also struggle to adapt across different graph distributions, including shifts in whether connected nodes tend to be similar.

The authors theoretically analyze these approaches and find that representation-level prompts essentially act like fine-tuning a simple downstream classifier. They use this result to motivate a division of responsibilities: prompting should draw out the pretrained model’s capabilities, while the classifier should adapt to the downstream scenario. This analysis gives the proposed method a specific rationale beyond choosing another prompt placement.

UniPrompt follows that principle while preserving the input graph. It is proposed as an adaptation method for arbitrary pretrained models, and experiments demonstrate integration with various pretrained models. The reported results show strong performance both within a domain and across domains. The empirical evidence supports broad compatibility across the models and scenarios evaluated, alongside the paper’s more general design aim.
neurips-2025-one-prompt-fits-all-univers.tldr: UniPrompt uses a theoretical analysis of graph prompts to guide adaptation across pretrained models and downstream domains while preserving the input graph.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can reconstruct compressed images using their learned knowledge of image structure, but repeated denoising makes decoding expensive. Training separate models for different bit-rates adds further training and storage costs. OSCAR addresses both costs with a single model that reconstructs images in one denoising step across multiple bit-rates.

The central idea is to view a compressed latent representation as a noisy version of the original latent. The distortion changes with the bit-rate, so OSCAR associates each rate with a pseudo diffusion timestep. This lets one generative model treat compressed representations as different intermediate points along a diffusion trajectory and condition reconstruction accordingly.

The authors argue that compressed latents retain enough structural information to make single-step denoising feasible. OSCAR uses that information directly instead of beginning an iterative reconstruction from random noise. Experiments report superior quantitative and visual reconstruction quality alongside substantially improved inference efficiency. The contribution connects compression strength to diffusion conditioning, making one shared decoder useful across rates while replacing repeated sampling with one pass.
neurips-2025-oscar-one-step-diffusion-co.tldr: OSCAR maps compression bit-rates to diffusion timesteps so one model can reconstruct images across rates with a single denoising pass.

paragraphs: PaceLLM addresses long-context understanding through two problems identified by the authors: useful internal activations fade, and unstructured feed-forward weights fragment semantic information. Its design takes inspiration from persistent neural activity and specialized cortical organization, translating those ideas into mechanisms for retaining and organizing language-model computation.

The Persistent Activity mechanism maintains an activation-level memory bank. It retrieves, reuses, and updates important feed-forward states so relevant information can remain available. Cortical Expert Clustering reorganizes feed-forward weights into semantic modules, establishing dependencies across tokens and reducing fragmentation. Together, the mechanisms target both the persistence of information and the organization of the computation that uses it.

Evaluations report a 6% improvement on LongBench’s multi-document question answering and gains of 12.5–17.5% on infinity-Bench tasks. Needle-In-A-Haystack tests extend measurable context length to 200,000 tokens. That length describes the reported retrieval test, while the other benchmarks assess broader tasks. The authors present the approach as broadly applicable and complementary to other methods, improving long-context performance and interpretability without requiring structural overhauls.
neurips-2025-pacellm-brain-inspired-larg.tldr: PaceLLM combines persistent activation memory with semantic grouping of feed-forward weights to improve long-context understanding.

paragraphs: Prediction with expert advice studies how a decision-maker learns from competing sources of advice over a sequence of decisions. The feedback used to assess those choices may contain noise, errors, or communication-related distortion. This paper focuses on additive noise: an extra random quantity corrupts the feedback available to the learner.

The analysis asks how much this corruption fundamentally affects regret, the performance measure used to assess sequential decisions against an expert benchmark. It develops sharp regret bounds for Gaussian noise, uniform noise, and a broader family of noise distributions with log-concave densities. The different cases allow the analysis to distinguish effects associated with the distribution of the noise.

The main finding is a characterization of how regret scales with properties of that distribution. This gives a more specific account of unreliable feedback than treating every noisy setting as equivalent. The contribution is theoretical: it establishes performance limits and sharp bounds for the analyzed noise settings, clarifying how the characteristics of corrupted observations affect what an online decision-maker can achieve.
neurips-2025-prediction-with-expert-advi.tldr: The paper derives sharp regret bounds showing how the distribution of additive feedback noise affects prediction with expert advice.

paragraphs: The geometric median finds a point minimizing the average distance to the data, providing a robust alternative to estimating a mean. Prior work achieved a differentially private approximation whose error depends on a radius containing most data points, rather than the worst-case radius. It also established an information-theoretically optimal sample requirement.

This paper retains that approximation quality and sample requirement while improving computation. For n points in d dimensions, the runtime is approximately nd plus d divided by the square of the approximation parameter, with logarithmic factors suppressed. The sample requirement scales as the square root of dimension divided by the product of the approximation and privacy parameters, matching the prior result.

The speedup combines subsampling and geometric aggregation to accelerate initialization with a custom sensitivity analysis of private stochastic gradient descent for the geometric median objective. The resulting runtime is nearly linear in the input size plus the cost of the cheapest non-private first-order method cited by the authors. The advance therefore concerns computational efficiency while preserving the established statistical and privacy guarantees.
neurips-2025-private-geometric-median-in.tldr: The paper speeds up differentially private geometric median estimation while preserving prior approximation quality and optimal sample requirements.

paragraphs: Complex questions can require several searches, with each result changing what should be investigated next. ReSearch trains language models to integrate this process into reasoning. Its focus is the interaction between thinking and information retrieval, especially when answering a question requires connecting evidence across multiple retrieval steps.

The framework uses reinforcement learning without supervised examples of reasoning steps. Text-based thinking guides when to search and how to formulate searches, while retrieved results inform the subsequent reasoning. Search operations become parts of the reasoning chain, allowing the model’s next action to depend on what earlier searches revealed.

The authors train Qwen2.5 models at the 7B and 32B scales, including their instruction-tuned variants. Although training uses only one dataset, the resulting models show strong generalization across several benchmarks. Their analysis also finds reflection and self-correction emerging during reinforcement learning. These findings suggest that training a model to coordinate reasoning with retrieval can produce useful search behavior and richer reasoning patterns without supplying labeled reasoning trajectories.
neurips-2025-research-learning-to-reason.tldr: ReSearch uses reinforcement learning to teach language models to interleave reasoning and search without supervised reasoning-step data.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning that seeks reliable long-term average reward despite uncertainty in the environment’s transition behavior. Distributional robustness evaluates policies against an uncertainty set of possible dynamics. The central question is how many samples are needed to estimate both a good policy and its robust average reward.

The authors give two algorithms. One reduces the problem to a distributionally robust discounted decision process. The other introduces an anchoring state to stabilize controlled transition kernels within the uncertainty set. Both attain the same near-optimal sample complexity, scaling with the number of state–action pairs, the square of the nominal mixing time, and the inverse square of the target accuracy, apart from logarithmic factors.

The guarantee assumes a uniformly ergodic nominal process and a sufficiently small uncertainty radius. It covers uncertainty sets based on KL and f_k divergences. These conditions define where the result applies. The authors describe it as the first finite-sample convergence guarantee for robust average-reward reinforcement learning and support the predicted convergence rates with numerical experiments.
neurips-2025-sample-complexity-of-distri.tldr: Two algorithms achieve near-optimal sample guarantees for robust long-term reinforcement learning under ergodicity and sufficiently small distributional uncertainty.

paragraphs: Clinical diagnosis unfolds as a sequence of decisions about what to investigate next. Models trained on fully observed, static datasets do not directly capture that process or its resource constraints. ACTMED frames diagnosis as adaptive test selection, using the information already available for an individual patient to guide the next step.

The framework combines Bayesian Experimental Design with language models. At each step, it selects the test expected to reduce diagnostic uncertainty most. Language models serve as simulators that generate plausible distributions over patient states and support updates to diagnostic beliefs, without requiring structured training data tailored to each task. The selection criterion concerns expected information gained before the test result is known.

Clinicians can review proposed tests, interpret intermediate outputs, and apply judgment throughout the process. Evaluations on real-world datasets show that ACTMED can improve diagnostic accuracy, interpretability, and resource use through test selection. The stated contribution is a step toward adaptive clinical support with less dependence on domain-specific data, combining explicit uncertainty-driven decisions with opportunities for clinician involvement.
neurips-2025-timely-clinical-diagnosis-t.tldr: ACTMED combines Bayesian experimental design and language-model simulation to select informative clinical tests sequentially while supporting clinician involvement.

paragraphs: Scheduling an Earth-observation constellation requires assigning imaging work while respecting satellite motion, available resources, and operational restrictions. Simplified scheduling settings can miss these interacting constraints. This paper supplies both a benchmark intended to capture realistic behavior and a scheduling model designed to account for the resulting limits.

AEOS-Bench contains 3,907 configured satellite assets and 16,410 scenarios. Each scenario includes between one and 50 satellites and between 50 and 300 imaging tasks. A high-fidelity simulator generates orbital dynamics and resource constraints, and each scenario includes ground-truth scheduling annotations. The benchmark provides a common evaluation setting for schedules involving different constellation sizes and workloads.

AEOS-Former is a Transformer-based scheduler with constraint-aware attention and an internal module explicitly representing physical and operational limits. It learns iteratively through simulation to adapt across scenarios. Experiments report better task completion and energy efficiency than baseline models, while ablations examine the contributions of individual components. The results support the proposed combination of realistic simulated evaluation and explicit constraint modeling for constellation scheduling.
neurips-2025-towards-realistic-earth-obs.tldr: AEOS-Bench and AEOS-Former pair realistic satellite scheduling scenarios with a constraint-aware model that improves task completion and energy efficiency.

paragraphs: Text-to-image diffusion models can produce harmful content in response to malicious prompts, reflecting concerns about inappropriate or biased training data. Safe Text embedding Guidance addresses output safety during generation. It changes the text representations conditioning the model, allowing an existing model to be guided without additional training.

At sampling time, STG evaluates a safety function on the expected final denoised image. That evaluation guides adjustments to the text embeddings. The method therefore links changes in prompt conditioning to an estimate of the eventual image, giving the generation process a safety-directed signal as sampling proceeds.

The authors theoretically show alignment of the underlying model distribution with safety constraints while minimally affecting generation quality. Experiments include nudity, violence, and artist-style removal. Across these scenarios, STG outperforms both training-based and training-free baselines at removing targeted content while preserving the prompt’s core semantic intent. The findings support modifying text conditioning as a practical intervention for safer generation, with the stated outcome being improved safety and retained meaning rather than an absolute guarantee against every harmful output.
neurips-2025-training-free-safe-text-emb.tldr: STG adjusts text embeddings during diffusion sampling to reduce unsafe content while preserving prompt meaning, without additional model training.

paragraphs: Continual learning often protects earlier tasks by restricting how new training changes the model. That protection can also prevent beneficial backward transfer: learning a strongly related new task may improve an older one. CaLoRA seeks such improvements with parameter-efficient adaptation in a setting where old-task data are unavailable.

Its first component, parameter-level counterfactual attribution, estimates the causal effects of LoRA parameters to identify those effective for task performance. Its second component, cross-task gradient adaptation, uses gradient projection to quantify task correlation and gradient similarity to assess affinity. Together, these signals guide adaptive changes to task gradients without replaying old data.

The approach addresses both ineffective parameter use and the difficulty of measuring relationships between tasks without shared historical examples. Across multiple benchmarks and continual-learning settings, CaLoRA outperforms state-of-the-art methods and better mitigates forgetting through positive backward transfer. The motivation is conditional on useful relationships between tasks; the reported results show that the framework can exploit such relationships, rather than establishing that every new task benefits every earlier one.
neurips-2025-turning-the-tables-enabling.tldr: CaLoRA combines counterfactual parameter attribution and task-gradient relationships to enable beneficial backward transfer without replaying old-task data.

paragraphs: Equivariant graph networks respect transformations of geometric inputs, but doing so does not by itself provide the ability to approximate every equivariant function. That stronger property is called completeness. Capturing the necessary interactions among multiple nodes can require costly depth, higher-order interactions, or richer transformation-aware features in existing approaches.

The paper proves that two components are sufficient to construct a complete equivariant graph network: a complete scalar function representing the graph’s canonical form, and a full-rank steerable basis. This separates the representation of geometric information from the basis used to express outputs that transform appropriately. The result provides a constructive route to completeness.

Using this characterization, the authors develop an efficient construction based on EGNN and TFN models. Empirical evaluations report strong completeness-related behavior and performance with only a few layers, reducing computational overhead. The theoretical contribution is the sufficient construction, while the experiments demonstrate its practical value. Together, they support obtaining expressive geometric models through the choice of representation and basis rather than relying only on architectural depth.
neurips-2025-universally-invariant-learn.tldr: The paper gives a sufficient construction for complete equivariant graph networks using a canonical scalar representation and a full-rank steerable basis.

paragraphs: A/B experiments compare alternatives as observations arrive, and investigators may want to stop once the evidence is convincing. Sequential tests support early stopping while controlling the risk of false discoveries. The paper identifies a trade-off in existing methods: some restrict how often results can be checked, while others have low statistical power.

YEAST introduces a test designed for continuous monitoring. Its derivation starts from a bound on the probability that a statistical process crosses a threshold. The authors obtain that bound using a classical maximal inequality and then invert it to construct the test. This connects the decision rule to the probability of crossing a boundary during monitoring.

Semi-synthetic simulations show that the proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art sequential testing approaches. The practical significance is a way to repeatedly examine an ongoing experiment while retaining the statistical rationale for stopping early. The paper’s contribution combines a new derivation technique with empirical evidence that the resulting test improves on existing approaches in the evaluated simulations.
neurips-2025-yeast-yet-another-sequentia.tldr: YEAST derives a continuously monitored A/B test from threshold-crossing bounds and outperforms existing sequential tests in semi-synthetic simulations.
